ANALYSIS OF SUPPLIED EVALUATIONS · 24 D4Ds · CBORG REFERENCE RESCORE, SEPTEMBER 12, 2026

Completeness, correctness,
and where review concerns concentrate

Historical cohort: September 2026. These reports describe frozen generic-v7/v8 records and their September 12 CBORG reference rescore, not the current generator or a current validation of its outputs. Saved render metadata dates v7 to September 1–2 and v8 to September 5 (VOICE replicate 1) or September 7 (the other 11 records). Labels beginning 2026-09-04f/g are run identifiers, not the generation dates of all v8 records. Provenance recording timestamps are distinct from exact model-call start times; see the saved VOICE v8 replicate 1 and CM4AI v8 replicate 2 records.

CM4AI generation-regime caveat. V8 replicates 2 and 3 returned no thinking block in the full, reconciliation, report, and report re-check phases. The historical requests omitted the thinking parameter; the generation analysis documents an input-correlated adaptive outcome, not an explicit request to disable thinking or an established proxy fault. Both replicate 2 and replicate 3 remain included in every original score and pooled result. The pooled CM4AI comparison therefore mixes observed thinking regimes. This limits attribution of differences to the v8 package alone; it does not establish that the regime explains any score difference or justify a corrected score.

AI_READI and VOICE have the highest recorded rubric scores, but every datasheet has at least one accuracy or correctness flag. Missing structured fields, information placed elsewhere, and unresolved source conflicts are recurring concerns. These figures summarize the evaluations and their source relationships; they do not certify the underlying datasets.

Interpretation boundary. The repository’s semantic audit qualifies 9 of 24 rubric20 Q19 rationales, identifies additional disputed CHORUS and CM4AI narratives, and records execution-permission and deadline changes. Scores are retained unchanged. Small version differences cannot establish improvement or select a winning run. Review labels are not verified error classes.

What the evaluations show

  • Coverage is not correctness. All 24 records receive a correctness or content-accuracy comment under at least one rubric. All four records scoring 5/5 on rubric20 Q1 also receive such flags. This is compatible with complete-looking documentation containing disputed mappings or source conflicts.
  • Two review types dominate: consistency (194/562, 34.5%) and completeness (189/562, 33.6%). Content accuracy contributes 65, correctness 58, and semantic understanding 56. Severity is 276 low, 230 medium, and 56 high, as labeled by the evaluators.
  • Common structural gaps: download_url (18/24 records), errata (15), imputation_protocols (13), and parent_datasets (12) are both unpopulated and named in completeness comments. A co-mentioned field can appear in this count even if it is not the main defect. These are not counts of mandatory-field violations.
  • Dataset-specific weaknesses: CHORUS has low rubric20 scores for maintenance (mean 40% of the item maximum) and bias documentation (47%). CM4AI loses points for file enumeration (50%) and software transparency (53%). AI_READI and VOICE are stronger overall but retain semantic and governance concerns.
  • No uniform v8 gain: CHORUS scores rise descriptively, AI_READI is nearly unchanged, and CM4AI and VOICE decline on the recorded means. The v8 generation package and evaluator execution boundaries prevent a clean single-factor interpretation.

These examples illustrate the reviewers’ claims. Even the native “correctness” category includes omissions, source defects, and disclosed inferences; it should not be read as a hallucination count.

PatternIllustrative review claimHow to interpret it

Common fields implicated: source_caveats (15/24), regulatory_restrictions (12), is_deidentified (10), and funders (9). source_caveats often documents uncertainty or correct handling of a source conflict, so its frequent appearance is not evidence that caveats themselves are wrong.

Exploratory statistical results

The tests below quantify associations in these generated records. They preserve dataset grouping and report effect sizes alongside raw p-values and Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-values (BH q). The analysis was selected after inspecting the data, so it is exploratory. No tested family has a BH-adjusted result below 0.05; this is not evidence that effects are absent.

Version differences

For each outcome, compare the three v8 records with the three v7 records within each dataset, then average the four dataset differences equally. An exact stratified permutation test enumerates all 20⁴ = 160,000 ways to assign three of six records to each version within each dataset. It assumes exchangeable generation replicates under the null, an assumption weakened by the documented execution changes. Qualified rubric20 totals remain qualified.

Outcomev8 − v7Raw pBH q (6 tests)
Completeness flags+0.92 comments / record0.46740.561
Accuracy/correctness flags+0.58 comments / record0.37100.557
Consistency flags+1.33 comments / record0.09250.278
Rubric10 adjusted score-0.59 pp0.57030.570
Rubric20 adjusted score-2.18 pp0.03440.206
Q1 completeness score+6.67 pp0.16000.320

The rubric20 decrease is −2.18 percentage points (raw p=0.0344, BH q=0.206). It is a descriptive decrease that does not pass the exploratory six-test adjustment, and the audit qualifications further limit interpretation. Q1 completeness rises by 6.67 points while consistency flags rise by 1.33 per record, illustrating that these features can move in different directions.

Completeness versus review flags, controlling dataset and version

Subtract each dataset × version group mean and correlate the remaining variation across generation replicates. Permute the outcome within the eight three-record groups (49,999 Monte Carlo permutations plus the observed allocation; seed 29092026). This tests within-group association rather than the difference between, for example, high-scoring AI_READI and lower-scoring CHORUS. Only four of eight groups vary in Q1, so information is limited.

Q1 completeness versusWithin-group Pearson rPermutation pBH q (3 tests)
Accuracy/correctness flags-0.1140.89081.000
Consistency flags+0.0570.85251.000

There is no detectable within-group association here between Q1 and accuracy/correctness flags (r=−0.114, p=0.891). This does not establish independence or show that completeness never relates to correctness; the Q1 scale is coarse and the sample is small.

Source-type associations within datasheet sections

For each source type, record, and section, compare the proportion of populated receipt-linked root fields receiving a review flag between (a) fields linked to that source type and (b) other receipt-linked fields in the same section. Both sets must be nonempty. Average eligible section contrasts equally within record, then records within dataset, then datasets. This accounts for broad section composition, but not field-specific difficulty, source overlap, or differences in claims within a root field.

  • Publication-linked fields: completeness-flag prevalence is 20.3 percentage points higher than the same-section comparison fields on average, positive in all three represented datasets (17 eligible records; exact sign-test p=0.25, BH q=0.60).
  • Data-resource-linked fields: accuracy/correctness-flag prevalence is 8.4 points higher, positive in all three represented datasets (18 records; p=0.25, q=0.60).
  • NIH-project-page-linked fields: consistency-flag prevalence is 11.9 points higher, positive in all four datasets (24 records; p=0.125, q=0.60).
  • Section mix changes the picture: the NIH-page completeness contrast is −12.8 points when all linked fields are compared within record, but +3.5 points when comparisons are restricted to eligible fields within the same section and sections are weighted equally. This changes the eligible comparison set as well as weighting; the shift shows why pooled source associations need qualification.

An exact two-sided sign test uses one averaged contrast per underlying dataset, rather than treating repeated generated records or individual fields as independent datasets. Types represented in fewer than three datasets are described in the data file but not tested. Four source types × three review outcomes give 12 tests, corrected as a family. With only three or four datasets, the smallest possible two-sided p-values are 0.25 and 0.125, respectively. This deliberately coarse test supports descriptions of direction and heterogeneity, not a claim of statistically established source-type differences. Its generalization assumes independent dataset contrasts with equally likely signs under the null; these four purposively selected projects are not a random sample of all datasets.

Claims supported by this analysis

Descriptive: “Completeness and consistency comments accounted for 68.1% of primary review issues. Every generated datasheet received at least one accuracy/correctness flag, including all four records receiving maximum Q1 completeness scores.”

Associational: “Source-linked fields exhibited different review-flag profiles across document types and datasheet sections. In within-section comparisons, publication-linked fields had a higher completeness-flag proportion in all three represented datasets, but the dataset-level test was underpowered and did not establish a statistically significant difference.”

Inferential: “Exploratory permutation tests did not detect a version difference after correction across six outcomes, nor a completeness–flag association conditional on dataset and version. These analyses concern recorded evaluator judgments, not independently verified factual error.”

Methods, scope, and reproducibility

The supplied folders contain exactly 32 rubric10 and 24 rubric20 JSON evaluations, all matching the repository’s accepted reference outputs byte-for-byte. Their 24 input YAML files match the evaluation manifest’s SHA-256 pins. Primary-score arithmetic and applicability denominators were checked for all 48 primary ratings. The analysis used local main commit d9e5c9dd0d1345b176918bdedaefcedad93f6012; no source download, new model evaluation, or alteration of source records was performed.

  • Units: 4 datasets × 2 generation versions × 3 replicates = 24 records. Two instruments yield 48 primary ratings. Eight extra rubric10 ratings are excluded from primary summaries. The six records per dataset are generated outputs, not six independent underlying datasets.
  • Instrument boundary: frozen evaluation scores and manifest identity are preserved. Current main contains later rubric edits; these were not applied retroactively. v8 is a generation configuration package, not an isolated one-rule intervention.
  • Missingness: figures distinguish raw completeness labels from actual unpopulated root fields. Structural absence does not prove applicability or availability in the source corpus. A populated field can contain an explicit negative statement, and an empty dedicated field can have equivalent information elsewhere.
  • Comment counts: only semantic_analysis.issues_detected is counted. Raw type/severity labels are preserved; native types overlap conceptually. Unique-record prevalence deduplicates the same field across rubrics but does not establish unique real-world errors.
  • Section mapping: an explicit, exported crosswalk uses current schema Dataset/Information fields and the defining module of each class range. Metadata is the fallback. This analytical crosswalk is not a re-evaluation under the current rubric.
  • Sources: receipt-declared extraction links, reconstructed from historical input bytes, describe intended support. Snippet entailment and final nested-field survival were not re-adjudicated. Source/review overlap uses only populated root fields and excludes 0 links to unpopulated roots. Unique root-field pairs suppress repeated snippets.
  • Uncertainty: no causal tests, source-type quality rankings, population confidence intervals, or accuracy percentages are justified here. Source type is confounded with dataset and documentation availability. Permission and deadline boundaries also confound version and repeat comparisons.
  • Known adjudication needs: Q19 is qualified for 9 rubric20 ratings. The CHORUS retry canary overstates license absence and alleges conflation despite an explicit distinction. The CM4AI pilot overlooks per-deposit version scope in Q13/Q19, overstates restrictions on participant-related documentation for cell-line work, and has donor/creator-count issues. Unflagged cases are not certified correct.

Recommended next analysis: adjudicate a stratified sample of review comments into (a) source fact absent, (b) extraction omission, (c) information misplaced, (d) disclosed source conflict, (e) unsupported or incorrect generated claim, and (f) reviewer error. Record supporting source spans and final D4D paths. That would support actual correctness rates and a defensible document-type error analysis; the present automated flags do not.

Audit sources and deliverables

Repository context used: notes/reference_rescore_2026-09-12_cborg_runtime/manifest.json, completion_summary.md, semantic_review.json, the generation prompts, schema modules, receipt_sources.py, the evaluated D4Ds, provenance records, and coverage receipts. Audit excerpts and qualifications are included in repository_qualifications.txt.

RecommendationReconcile the release-level version string with the Dataverse version numbers of the prior releases, or state explicitly in version_access that Dataverse version numbers are per-deposit and are not a monotonic sequence across the CM4AI release series.
